intro.title: The German alphabet, special sounds and spelling your name
explanation: German has 26 letters like English, plus ä, ö, ü and ß. The letter names are different, so learn them from the table. You need them to spell your name (buchstabieren), for example on the phone.

Some letters sound different from English. W sounds like English v (Wasser), V often sounds like f (Vater), and Z sounds like ts (Zahl). Ei sounds like English eye (heißen), and ie sounds like ee (Wiedersehen).

Ch, sch and tsch are different sounds. Sch sounds like English sh (Schule). Tsch sounds like English ch in church (Tschüs, Deutsch). Ä, ö and ü are changed vowels called Umlaute, and ß is a sharp s sound, like ss (heißen).
To greet someone and ask their name, use Hallo, Wie heißt du? and Ich heiße ... To say goodbye, use Tschüs or Auf Wiedersehen.
intro.rule_summary: Learn the letter names, spell names letter by letter, and keep tsch (like English ch) apart from sch (like English sh).

culture.title: Hello and goodbye in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often greet each other when they enter a small shop, a waiting room or a lift. A short Guten Tag! or Hallo! is polite. Many people use Guten Morgen! in the morning, and Guten Abend! in the evening. With friends and young people, Hallo! and Tschüs! are very common. With adults you do not know, people use Sie and often say Auf Wiedersehen! when they leave. In Switzerland you may hear different greetings, and in southern Germany and Austria people often say Servus or Grüß Gott. You do not need to use these yet, but it is nice to recognise them. Names are often spelled aloud on the phone, so the alphabet is very useful.
culture.reflection_question: How do you usually greet people and say goodbye in your own language, and is it different for friends and for strangers?

mission.title: Spell your name like a German speaker
mission.task: Practise greeting and spelling your name out loud today, as you would in a real situation, for example on the phone or at a reception desk.
steps: Stand in front of a mirror or record yourself on your phone. Say: Hallo! Ich heiße ... (your name).
Say the letter names of your first name slowly, one by one. Then say the sentence Wie schreibt man das? and spell your name again.
Say Guten Morgen!, Guten Tag! or Guten Abend! to match the time of day. Then say Tschüs! and Auf Wiedersehen! and listen carefully: tsch in Tschüs sounds like English "ch", not like "sh".

mission.safety_note: Practise only with your own name. Do not share private details such as your address or phone number in recordings or with strangers online.

intro.title: Personal pronouns + sein; Ich heiße… / Ich bin… / Ich komme aus…
explanation: Personal pronouns tell us who is speaking or who we are talking about: ich (I), du (you, a friend), er (he), sie (she), es (it), wir (we), ihr (you, several friends), sie (they) and Sie (you, formal). The formal Sie always has a capital S.
The verb sein (to be) is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist. You use it for names, feelings and states: Ich bin Anna. Ich bin müde.
To say your name you can use heißen: Ich heiße Jonas. To say where you are from, use kommen + aus: Ich komme aus Deutschland.
To say how you feel, do not use 'Ich bin gut'. Say Mir geht es gut. The question is Wie geht es dir?
intro.rule_summary: ich bin / du bist / er ist; Ich heiße… = my name; Ich komme aus… = where I am from; Mir geht es gut = I am fine.

culture.title: Du or Sie? Introducing yourself
culture.note: In German-speaking countries, people choose between du and Sie. You use du with friends, family, children and fellow students. You use Sie with adults you do not know well, at work and in shops. Sie always has a capital S. When you are not sure, start with Sie. People often say their first name and sometimes their last name when they meet, for example "Ich heiße Anna." Often people shake hands in a formal situation. In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people also say where they live or where they are from, but this is not required. If someone says "Wir können du sagen", it means you can now use du.

intro.title: Numbers 0–100, phone numbers and age
explanation: Learn 0–12 as separate words: null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf. From 13 to 19 you say the small number plus -zehn: dreizehn, vierzehn. Watch the changes: sechzehn (not sechszehn) and siebzehn (not siebenzehn).

From 21 on, German says the small number FIRST: 21 = einundzwanzig, which is literally 'one-and-twenty'. You write it as one long word: ein + und + zwanzig. Note that 1 becomes ein- inside the word. The tens are zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig, hundert.
For a phone number, say each digit one by one: 0151 = null eins fünf eins. Take a short pause between groups. For age, German uses sein, not haben: Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt. Ask: Wie alt bist du?

culture.title: Phone numbers in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often say phone numbers in small groups of digits or in pairs, for example "vierundfünfzig" for 54. Some people say each digit alone. Zero is "null". When you give a number, people often repeat it to be sure. Mobile numbers are long, so it is normal to say them slowly. If you do not understand, you can say "Noch einmal, bitte." People write the house number after the street name: "Lindenstraße 12". The postcode (Postleitzahl) comes before the city name, for example "10115 Berlin". Germany uses the euro. Switzerland uses its own money, the Swiss franc.

intro.title: Regular verbs in the present tense
explanation: German verbs in the dictionary form end in -en: wohnen, lernen, arbeiten, spielen. To use a verb, take off -en. What is left is the stem: wohn-, lern-, arbeit-, spiel-.
Then add an ending that matches the person: ich wohne, du wohnst, er wohnt, wir wohnen, ihr wohnt, sie wohnen. The verb changes, so you always need the right ending.
One present tense is enough: Ich wohne in Berlin means both 'I live in Berlin' and 'I am living in Berlin'.
If the stem ends in -t (arbeit-), add an extra e before -st and -t so it is easy to say: du arbeitest, er arbeitet, ihr arbeitet.
intro.rule_summary: Stem + ending: -e (ich), -st (du), -t (er/sie/es, ihr), -en (wir, sie/Sie); with a stem ending in -t, add -e- before -st and -t.

culture.title: Living and studying in Germany
culture.note: Many students in Germany do not live with their family. Some students live in a Wohnung with other students. This is called a WG (say: "Veh-Geh"), short for Wohngemeinschaft. Each person has their own Zimmer, and they share the kitchen and the bathroom. Other students live in a student residence or alone. Many cities have a big Universität, and students often come from different towns and countries. Students often ride a bike or take the bus to the Kurs. At many universities, students pay a small fee every semester, but often no high course fees. A WG is popular because rooms in big cities can be expensive.

culture.title: Du or Sie when you meet someone
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people choose between du and Sie when they ask questions. Children, family, friends and most students say du to each other. Adults who do not know each other well, for example in a shop, in an office or at work, usually say Sie. With Sie, the question sounds like this: Wie heißen Sie? Woher kommen Sie? Sie always has a capital S. If you are not sure, start with Sie. Often the other person then says: Wir können du sagen. That means you can both use du. At a language course, people often ask the same first questions: name, country, city and languages. It is normal and friendly to ask them.

intro.title: The verb always comes second
explanation: In a German statement, the conjugated verb always stands in position 2. Position 1 can be the subject (Ich lerne heute Deutsch.) or something else, such as a time word (Heute lerne ich Deutsch.).
Position 1 can be one word or a short group of words that belong together, for example 'Am Montag' or 'Im Sommer'. Count the whole group as one position. The verb comes right after it.
If you put a time word first, the subject moves behind the verb. So it is 'Heute lerne ich', not 'Heute ich lerne'. The meaning stays the same, only the focus changes.
Use am for days (am Montag) and im for months and seasons (im Mai, im Sommer).
intro.rule_summary: Position 1 (subject or time) + verb in position 2 + the rest: Heute lerne ich Deutsch.

culture.title: Weekdays, weekends and the four seasons
culture.note: In Germany, the week starts on Monday, and most calendars show Monday as the first day. Many people work from Monday to Friday, so Samstag and Sonntag are the Wochenende. On Sundays most shops are closed, so people often rest, walk, or meet family and friends. Germany has four clear seasons: Frühling, Sommer, Herbst and Winter. Summer is usually warm and winter is often cold. Many people use a paper or phone Kalender to plan their days. When you say goodbye on Friday, you can say: Schönes Wochenende!

intro.title: Telling the time, and 'um' and 'am' for when
explanation: To ask the time, say 'Wie spät ist es?' To answer, say 'Es ist ... Uhr.' For example: 'Es ist drei Uhr.' For one o'clock, say 'ein Uhr' (not 'eins Uhr').

There are two ways to say the time. In everyday speech (informal) we use 'nach' (past), 'vor' (to), 'Viertel' (quarter) and 'halb' (half). On trains, at work and in announcements (formal) we use the 24-hour clock: 'Es ist fünfzehn Uhr dreißig.' Careful: 'halb vier' means 3:30, half an hour on the way to four.

To say when you do something, use 'um' with a clock time: 'um sieben Uhr' (at seven o'clock). Use 'am' with a part of the day or a day of the week: 'am Morgen', 'am Abend', 'am Montag'. The question is 'Wann ...?' (When ...?). The verb stays in second place: 'Anna frühstückt um sieben Uhr.' / 'Um sieben Uhr frühstückt Anna.'

culture.title: Clocks and being on time
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, punctuality is important. People usually arrive on time for work, school, doctor's appointments and trains. If you will be late, it is polite to call or write a message. In writing, on timetables and in formal situations, people often use the 24-hour clock, for example 14:30. In everyday speech, many people use the 12-hour clock and say 'halb drei'. Be careful: halb drei does not mean 'half past three' (like 'half three' in British English). It means half way to three, so it is 2:30. Many people also say 'Viertel nach' or 'Viertel vor' for quarter past and quarter to. Listening to how people say the time at the station or on the radio is great practice.

intro.title: Articles: Nominativ and Akkusativ
explanation: Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). In the plural, all nouns use die. The article shows the gender, so learn each noun together with its article: der Vater, die Mutter, das Kind.

The Nominativ is the case of the subject, the person or thing that does the action. It is also used after sein: Der Vater ist nett. Das ist ein Bruder. The Akkusativ is the case of the direct object, for example after haben (I have) or sehen (I see): Ich habe einen Bruder.
Only the masculine changes from Nominativ to Akkusativ: der becomes den, and ein becomes einen. Feminine (die, eine), neuter (das, ein) and plural (die) stay the same.
intro.rule_summary: Nominativ = subject (and after sein); Akkusativ = object (after haben, sehen): only masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen.

examples.note: Object of haben: Akkusativ, ein → einen.
Feminine does not change: eine Schwester.
Object of sehen: der Vater → den Vater.
Neuter does not change: ein Kind.

culture.title: Family in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people live in small households: a single person, a couple, or parents with one or two children. Grandparents often live in another town, so families often meet on weekends, on birthdays and at holidays. Many families have coffee and cake together on Sunday afternoon. When Germans talk about the family, they often say die Familie for parents and children, and die Verwandten for relatives such as Onkel, Tante, Cousin and Cousine. Families are very different, and many children also have step-parents or live with one parent. In everyday speech, many people say Oma and Opa for grandparents, and Mama and Papa for parents.

intro.title: Saying no: nicht or kein?
explanation: German has two main words for negation. Use kein (a form of ein) to negate a noun that has ein/eine or no article at all: Ich habe einen Balkon. → Ich habe keinen Balkon. Kein takes the endings of ein: kein, keine, keinen.
Use nicht for everything else: to negate a verb, an adjective, or a noun with a definite article (der, die, das) or with mein/dein: Das Bad ist nicht groß. Lena kauft den Tisch nicht.

Nicht usually goes at the end of a short sentence. Before an adjective it stands directly in front of it: nicht groß. Kein stands right before the noun and changes like ein (masculine accusative: keinen).
intro.rule_summary: ein-noun or no article → kein/keine/keinen + noun; verb, adjective or der/die/das-noun → nicht.

culture.title: Renting a flat in Germany
culture.note: Many people in Germany, Austria and Switzerland rent their home instead of buying it. The monthly rent is called die Miete. You often see two prices: Kaltmiete (rent only) and Warmmiete (rent plus costs such as heating). Some empty flats come without a kitchen, so tenants bring or buy their own. In many buildings, names are written next to the doorbell at the front door. Most buildings also have quiet hours, often at night and on Sundays, when people try not to make noise. Rules differ between buildings, so it is polite to check the house rules (die Hausordnung).

intro.title: Dative articles: dem, der, dem, den
explanation: In German the noun's job in the sentence changes the article. After some small words (prepositions) like mit, bei, von, zu and aus, and after the verb geben (to give) for the person who receives something, you use the dative case.
The dative articles are: masculine dem, feminine der, neuter dem, plural den. Compare: der Verkäufer becomes dem Verkäufer, die Karte becomes der Karte, das Geld becomes dem Geld.
In the plural, the noun usually also gets an -n: die Kinder becomes mit den Kindern. If the plural already ends in -n (die Kunden), nothing is added.
The same pattern works with ein and kein: einem, einer, einem. Some short forms are very common: bei + dem = beim, zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, von + dem = vom.
intro.rule_summary: Dative: der → dem, die → der, das → dem, plural die → den (+n); ein → einem, eine → einer; used after mit, bei, von, zu, aus and for the person who receives (geben).

culture.title: Shopping in Germany
culture.note: In Germany many people buy bread at a Bäcker and fresh fruit and vegetables at a market or in a supermarket. Most shops close on Sundays, so people often shop on Saturday. At the supermarket checkout, you usually put your things on the belt and pack them yourself, often in your own Tasche, because plastic bags usually cost extra. Many shops accept a Karte, but some small bakeries and market stalls prefer cash, so it is useful to ask: Kann ich mit der Karte bezahlen? Greeting the Verkäufer or the Verkäuferin with Guten Tag and saying Bitte and Danke is polite and normal.

intro.title: Possessive articles: mein, dein, sein, ihr
explanation: A possessive article shows who something belongs to: mein Bus (my bus), dein Park (your park). The stem depends on the owner: ich = mein, du = dein, er/es = sein, sie = ihr, wir = unser, ihr = euer, Sie = Ihr.
The ending depends on the noun that follows: its gender, its number and its case. The endings are the same as for ein/eine/ein (and kein): mein Bahnhof, meine Straße, mein Haus, meine Freunde.

In the nominative (the subject) the masculine and neuter forms have no ending. In the accusative (the direct object) only the masculine changes: Ich sehe meinen Bahnhof. In the dative (after mit, bei, zu, in for where?) the endings are -em, -er, -em, -en: mit meinem Bus, mit meiner Freundin.
In the dative plural the noun also usually gets -n: bei meinen Eltern. Remember: sein = his, ihr = her. The owner decides the stem, not the noun.
intro.rule_summary: Stem = owner (mein, dein, sein, ihr); ending = noun's gender and case, like ein: Nom mein/meine/mein, Akk meinen/meine/mein, Dat meinem/meiner/meinem.

culture.title: Getting around the city
culture.note: In many German, Austrian and Swiss cities, people use buses, trams, trains and bicycles every day. You often buy a ticket at a machine or in an app, and in some cities you must validate a paper ticket before you ride. Cities usually have a Bahnhof in the centre, and many streets have bike lanes. Many people live in flats, so they often tell friends their street and house number, for example: Ich wohne in der Bahnhofstraße 5. Shops such as a Bäcker or an Apotheke are often close to a Haltestelle, so you can do errands on foot. Public transport timetables are often very precise, and people like to be on time when they meet a friend at a stop.

intro.title: The imperative: telling someone what to do (du / ihr / Sie)
explanation: German has three imperative forms, depending on who you talk to. For du, take the verb stem (the infinitive without -en): kommen becomes Komm! For ihr, use the ihr form of the verb without the word ihr: Kommt! For the formal Sie, put the verb first and keep Sie: Kommen Sie!
Some verbs change their vowel in the du-form (e to i or ie): sprechen becomes Sprich!, lesen becomes Lies!. The verb sein is irregular: Sei pünktlich! / Seid pünktlich! / Seien Sie pünktlich!
Separable verbs put the prefix at the end: anrufen becomes Ruf mich an! / Ruft mich an! / Rufen Sie mich an! Add bitte to be polite: Warte bitte kurz.
intro.rule_summary: du: stem (Komm!) · ihr: ihr-form without ihr (Kommt!) · Sie: infinitive + Sie (Kommen Sie!); sein: Sei / Seid / Seien Sie.

culture.title: Being on time in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, being on time is usually seen as a sign of respect. For a doctor's appointment, a meeting at work or a train, people try to arrive a few minutes early. If you will be late, it is polite to call or write a message before the appointment. In daily life, people often say a time like "um halb drei". Careful: halb drei means 2:30, not 3:30, because it is half an hour before three. Many people also use the 24-hour clock in writing and official announcements, for example 14:30 on a train timetable, but in speech they often say "halb drei". Among friends, a small delay of a few minutes can be fine at a private party, but for appointments it is better to be punctual.

intro.title: Irregular Partizip II: the 40 verbs you need for travel stories
explanation: You already know the Perfekt: a form of haben or sein in second position, and the Partizip II at the end of the sentence. Regular verbs end in -t (gemacht). Many very common verbs are irregular. Their Partizip II usually ends in -en (gesehen, gefahren), and often the vowel in the stem changes (trinken, getrunken). You have to learn these forms by heart.

Most irregular verbs form the Perfekt with haben: Ich habe ein Buch gelesen. Verbs of movement or change of place (fahren, fliegen, gehen, kommen) and the verbs sein and bleiben use sein: Wir sind nach Rom geflogen. The forms of the verb are the same as for the regular ones, only the Partizip II is new.

A small group of mixed verbs has the regular ending -t but also changes its stem: bringen, gebracht. Learn them as a separate group. Verbs with a separable prefix put ge- in the middle: ankommen, angekommen; einsteigen, eingestiegen. The verb bekommen and the verb beginnen have no ge-: bekommen, begonnen.
intro.rule_summary: haben/sein + Partizip II at the end; irregular Partizip II usually ends in -en with a changed stem (gesehen, gefahren); movement verbs, sein and bleiben take sein.

culture.title: Travelling by train
culture.note: Trains are a very common way to travel in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. Many cities have a Bahnhof in the centre, and you can often walk or take a bus from there to your hotel. Timetables show the Gleis, which is the platform number where your train leaves. It is a good idea to check it before you go, because it can change. Many people buy a Fahrkarte on a phone or at a machine in the station. Trains are often on time, but sometimes they are late, so many travellers plan some extra minutes for changing trains. On long journeys, people read, listen to music or look at the landscape through the window.

intro.title: Perfekt with separable and inseparable verbs
explanation: The Perfekt has two parts: haben (or sein) in second position and the participle (Partizip II) at the end. Regular verbs form the participle as ge- + stem + -t: arbeiten → gearbeitet.
Separable verbs have a prefix such as an-, auf-, ein-, mit- or ab-. In the participle, ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: anrufen → angerufen, aufräumen → aufgeräumt, einkaufen → eingekauft.
Inseparable verbs start with be-, ver-, er-, ent- or zer-. They get no ge- at all: besuchen → besucht, verstehen → verstanden, bekommen → bekommen.
Most verbs use haben. Verbs of movement or change of place or state, such as ankommen, aufstehen and mitkommen, use sein: Lena ist angekommen.
intro.rule_summary: Separable: prefix + ge + stem (angerufen); inseparable: no ge- (besucht); most verbs take haben, movement verbs like ankommen take sein.

pronunciation.focus: Stress in separable and inseparable verbs
pronunciation.explanation: In separable verbs the stress is on the prefix: AN-gerufen. In inseparable verbs the prefix is unstressed and the stress falls on the stem: be-SUCHT. The unstressed ge- and be- are short and weak.

words.hint: AUF-ge-räumt: stress AUF; äu sounds like English oy.
EIN-ge-kauft: stress EIN, which sounds like English eye-n.
be-SUCHT: stress the second syllable; ch as in Bach.
fer-SHTAN-den: stress STAN; v sounds like f, st like sht.
be-ZAHLT: stress ZAHLT; z sounds like ts and ah is long.

culture.title: Working hours and punctuality in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, being on time at work is very important. If you have an appointment (ein Termin) or a meeting (eine Besprechung), you usually arrive a few minutes early. If you are going to be late, you call or write an e-mail and say so. Many offices also offer flexible working hours, but a fixed time for meetings is still normal. Colleagues often greet each other in the morning with Guten Morgen or Hallo. In many companies, colleagues use du with each other, but with customers and with the boss people often use Sie. If you are not sure, start with Sie. Breaks are also common: many people take a short break for lunch or coffee with colleagues.

intro.title: Time expressions: am, um, im, seit, vor
explanation: German uses small words to say when something happens. Use am with days, dates and parts of the day (am Samstag, am 5. Mai, am Abend). Use um with clock times (um acht Uhr). Use im with months and seasons (im Mai, im Sommer).
Use seit for something that started in the past and is still true now: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier. Use vor for something that happened a certain time ago: Die Party war vor einer Woche.

After seit and vor the next word changes: einem Jahr, einer Woche, zwei Tagen. Learn these as fixed chunks at A1: seit einem Jahr, seit einer Woche, vor einem Jahr, vor einer Woche, vor zwei Tagen. With a day or month there is no change: seit Montag, seit Juni.
intro.rule_summary: am = day, date, part of the day; um = clock time; im = month, season; seit = since / for (still going on); vor = ago.

culture.title: Silvester and Karneval
culture.note: In Germany, people celebrate Silvester on the evening of 31 December. Many meet friends, eat together and watch the Feuerwerk at midnight. Some people also say "Guten Rutsch!", which means a good start into the new year. Another big party time is Karneval, which is especially popular in some regions in the west and south of Germany. It takes place in winter or early spring. People wear costumes, dance in the streets and watch parades. Not every region celebrates Karneval, and in some places it is called Fasching or Fastnacht. For a birthday, many people invite friends and family and often bring a small Geschenk. The birthday person often brings the Kuchen or the drinks to work or school.

intro.title: Prepositions with the accusative: für, durch, ohne, gegen, um
explanation: Some German prepositions are always followed by the accusative case. Five important ones are für (for), durch (through), ohne (without), gegen (against, into) and um (around). You never have to think about 'where' or 'whether something moves'; these five always take the accusative.
In the accusative only the masculine nouns change: der becomes den and ein becomes einen. Feminine, neuter and plural nouns look the same as in the nominative: die Lampe, das Bett, die Stühle.
After ohne you often use no article at all when you mean 'without any': ohne Kissen. If you want to say 'without the pillow', use ohne das Kissen.
intro.rule_summary: für, durch, ohne, gegen, um + accusative: der → den, ein → einen; die, das and plural stay the same.

intro.title: Two-way prepositions: Wo? or Wohin?
explanation: Some prepositions, like in, an, auf, vor, hinter and neben, can take the dative or the accusative. They are called two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen). The question decides the case.

Wo? asks about a place, with no change of place: Wo ist der Bus? You use the dative: Der Bus ist an der Haltestelle. Wohin? asks about a movement or a direction: Wohin fährst du? You use the accusative: Ich fahre in die Stadt.

The article changes in all three genders: der becomes dem for Wo? and den for Wohin?; das becomes dem for Wo? and stays das for Wohin?; die becomes der for Wo? and stays die for Wohin?. Often in dem becomes im and an dem becomes am.
intro.rule_summary: Wo? (place, no movement) = dative: in der / auf dem / an dem. Wohin? (movement, direction) = accusative: in die / auf den / an das.

culture.title: Tickets and Trust on German Public Transport
culture.note: In many German cities, buses, trams and trains work with a ticket system that relies on trust. Often there is no barrier at the stop, and you can simply walk onto the platform or into the vehicle. However, there are random ticket checks, and people without a valid ticket must pay a fine. So you should buy your ticket before you travel, or validate it if it needs a stamp. Many people use a monthly ticket or a ticket on their phone. Timetables are shown at the stop, and trains often leave from a numbered Gleis. Punctuality is valued, but delays can happen, so it is useful to check the display at the Haltestelle or the Bahnhof.

intro.title: Putting things somewhere or being somewhere: stellen/stehen, legen/liegen, hängen
explanation: German has two kinds of verbs for position. One kind is an action: you put something somewhere (Wohin?). The other kind is a state: something is somewhere (Wo?). stellen = to put upright, legen = to lay flat, hängen = to hang up. These answer Wohin? and use the accusative: Ich lege den Ausweis auf den Tisch.

The state verbs are stehen (upright), liegen (flat) and hängen (hanging). They answer Wo? and use the dative: Der Ausweis liegt auf dem Tisch. Note that hängen is used for both: Ich hänge die Jacke an den Haken (action). Die Jacke hängt am Haken (state).
The little words auf, an, in and neben change the case. Wohin? = accusative (den Tisch, die Tasche). Wo? = dative (dem Tisch, der Tasche). Learn the pairs as blocks: auf den Tisch / auf dem Tisch.
Do not mix up the verbs: legen and stellen need a person who does something (Ich lege ...). liegen and stehen just describe where something is (Der Pass liegt ...).
intro.rule_summary: Wohin? = stellen / legen / hängen + accusative; Wo? = stehen / liegen / hängen + dative.

culture.title: Anmeldung at the Einwohnermeldeamt
culture.note: In Germany, people who move into a new home must register their address, usually within two weeks. This is called die Anmeldung. You go to a local office, often called Einwohnermeldeamt or Bürgeramt. In many cities you need a Termin, so you book a time online or by phone. Often you bring your Ausweis or passport, a filled-in Formular and a confirmation from your landlord. At the Schalter or in an office, an employee checks your documents and enters your new Adresse. Rules and details can differ between cities and countries, so check the website of your local office first. Austria and Switzerland also have registration, but the offices and the deadlines are different.

intro.title: A1 review: the building blocks of simple German
explanation: In a German statement the verb is always in second position: Jonas wohnt in Berlin. If you put another word first, the verb stays second: In Berlin wohnt Jonas. In a W-question (wer, wo, woher, wie) the question word comes first and the verb second: Woher kommst du?

Regular verbs take endings that match the person: ich -e, du -st, er/sie -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. The two most important verbs, sein and haben, are irregular. Use sein for names, origin, feelings and age (Ich bin 25). Use haben for Hunger, Durst and things you own (Ich habe Durst).

Nouns have a gender (der, die, das) and a plural, so learn each noun with its article. Negate a noun with kein/keine (Ich habe keine Zeit) and everything else with nicht (Ich komme nicht aus Spanien). Use du with friends and family, and Sie (capital S) with adults you do not know well.
intro.rule_summary: Verb in second position, endings match the person, learn nouns with their article, kein for nouns, nicht for the rest, du for friends and Sie for formal situations.

culture.title: Registering your address in Germany
culture.note: In Germany, people who move into a new flat usually have to register their new address at the local registration office. This is called the "Anmeldung". It normally has to be done within two weeks of moving in. Many offices ask you to book an appointment (einen Termin) first. You often bring your ID (der Ausweis), a filled-in form (das Formular) and a confirmation from your landlord. Rules and details can differ between cities and between countries such as Austria and Switzerland, so check the website of your local office. Because of this step, German forms often ask for your name, your address and your signature (die Unterschrift). At the counter, officials are usually addressed with Sie, so the polite form is a good habit from day one.
culture.reflection_question: How do people register their address in your country, and what documents do they need?

mission.title: My German mini-profile
mission.task: Write and say a short introduction of yourself in German using the building blocks of this review. Practise it aloud, as if you were at a registration desk or meeting a new neighbour.
steps: Write 5 short German sentences: your name, where you come from, where you live, what you do and one thing you like (for example: Ich heiße ... Ich komme aus ... Ich wohne in ... Ich arbeite ... Ich trinke gern Wasser.).
Add one sentence with "kein" or "nicht" (for example: Ich habe heute keine Zeit. or Ich arbeite heute nicht.).
Say your sentences aloud twice. Practise the sounds sch, tsch and st/sp in words such as Schule, Deutsch, Stadt and sprechen.
Then say them again in the polite form, as if someone asked you: Woher kommen Sie?
mission.report_prompt: Write your 5 to 6 German sentences and tell us which one was hardest to say aloud and why.
success_check: I wrote sentences with the verb in second position.
I used the correct verb endings for ich and for Sie.
I used kein with a noun or nicht correctly in one sentence.
mission.safety_note: Do not share private data such as your full address, phone number or ID number in your report. Use a general city name only.
